n: Isaac now willingly blesses Jacob, knowing who he is, and charges him not to marry a Canaanite woman. The blessing is confirmed openly.

f.w: Thou shalt not take a wife of the daughters of Canaan

n: Isaac sends Jacob to his mother’s family in Paddan-aram to marry one of Laban’s daughters, as Abraham once sent for Rebekah.
Isaac blesses Jacob in the name of God Almighty (El Shaddai), the name God used when He made His covenant with Abraham.

f.g: Hebrew qehal ʿammim—an assembly or congregation of peoples.

n: Isaac passes on “the blessing of Abraham”—the covenant promises of posterity, land, priesthood, and blessing to the world. Latter-day Saints seek these same blessings through temple covenants.
Jacob leaves for Paddan-aram to his uncle Laban. The narrator notes Rebekah is mother of both Jacob and Esau—a reminder of the family’s pain.
Esau notices that Jacob was blessed and sent to marry within the family.
Esau sees that Jacob obeyed his parents.

f.w: obeyed his father and his mother

n: Esau realizes his Canaanite wives displease his father.
Trying to win approval, Esau marries a daughter of Ishmael. He adds a wife rather than changing his heart, and he chooses from the line that had been sent away.
Jacob sets out alone from Beersheba toward Haran, a journey of about 500 miles. He flees with little, unlike Abraham’s servant who traveled with ten camels.
At sunset he stops at a certain place and sleeps outdoors with a stone for a headrest. He is alone, vulnerable, and far from home.

f.g: Literally “the place”—hinting it is a special, sacred spot.

n: Jacob dreams of a stairway reaching from earth to heaven with angels going up and down. Heaven and earth are connected. Jesus later applied this image to Himself, and many Latter-day Saints see in it the steps of temple covenants leading back to God.

f.g: Hebrew sullam—a stairway or ramp, perhaps like the stepped sides of a ziggurat.

n: The Lord stands above the stairway and introduces Himself as the God of Abraham and Isaac. He promises Jacob the land on which he lies.

f.w: the LORD God of Abraham thy father, and the God of Isaac

n: God renews the Abrahamic covenant with Jacob: countless descendants spreading in every direction, and blessing for all the world’s families through him.

f.w: as the dust of the earth
in thy seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed

n: God promises to be with Jacob everywhere, protect him, bring him home, and never leave him. These words would sustain Jacob through twenty hard years.
Jacob wakes in awe: the Lord was here, and he had not realized it. God can meet us in unexpected places.

f.w: Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not

n: Filled with reverent fear, Jacob calls the place the house of God and gate of heaven—the essence of what a temple is.

f.g: Ironically what Babel claimed to be (Bab-ili, “gate of god”); here God Himself provides it.

n: Early in the morning Jacob sets up his stone as a pillar and anoints it with oil, consecrating the place as holy.

f.g: A standing stone set up as a memorial.

f.w: poured oil upon the top of it

n: He names the place Bethel, “house of God”; the town nearby was called Luz.
Jacob makes a vow: if God protects him and provides food and clothing on his journey…

f.g: Made a solemn promise to God.

f.w: bread to eat, and raiment to put on

n: …and brings him safely home, then the Lord will be his God. Jacob’s “if” may reflect early, growing faith—or a humble acceptance of God’s own promises.

f.w: then shall the LORD be my God

n: Jacob promises that the stone will mark God’s house and that he will give God a tenth of all he receives—following Abraham’s example of tithing.

f.w: I will surely give the tenth unto thee
